verdict: This is a coin-flip decided by half a pixel, which is a damning thing to have to say about two carets. Both are the same 3×36 CSS px slab of #00B5FF with square ends and zero antialiasing — the same instrument, not two designs. A wins only because its stems and its caret land on the same pixel grid, so the caret's top edge and the ascenders agree; in B the glyphs sit a half-pixel low and slightly fogged at the baseline, so the hard blue bar looks pasted onto the line rather than standing in it. Neither shows a selection at all, so half of what was supposed to be judged here simply isn't on screen.

states.name: selection
states.gap: B's caret line-start column is not stable: x=601 on '##' lines, 625 on '#', 630 on '- ', versus 673 on all body lines — up to 72 device px (36 CSS px) of lateral throw. Arrowing up from prose into a heading, or hitting Home on a list item, flings the caret out of the text column into the margin; A holds every one of its 18 line-starts within 673-678 (±5px).
states.gapTheirs: A's caret has no single column to return to: markers sit inside the prose column at x=673, so heading and list-item glyphs start at x=721 while body glyphs start at 673 — a 48px (24 CSS px) ragged text edge. The caret's line-start position is constant only because it is parked on '#'/'##'/'- ' markup occupying the writing column; on any structural line the caret must cross 2-3 character cells (~51-77px at 25.7px/cell) of syntax that shares the column with prose, and the caret gives zero positional signal about what kind of line it is on.
states.verdict: Neither of these carets is an instrument — they are the same 3px hard-edged sky-blue slab, unrounded, unantialiased, spanning the full 72px line box against 38px of glyph ink, which means roughly 47% of the bar is empty leading stabbing above the ascender and below the descender. Both also draw a full-opacity caret at BOTH ends of the selection (cols 942-947 and 1404-1409), a mobile drag-handle idiom; a writer looks for the one caret that marks where the next character lands and finds two candidates. B wins only because it keeps the prose column flush at 673 and hangs the markup at 601/625/630, so the caret's home for actual words never moves and its position on a structural line reads as structure; A buys caret-column stability by stuffing '#' and '- ' into the writing column, which leaves the text itself ragged by 48px. This is a tiebreak on placement, not on caret craft — on caret craft they are the same pixels, and both are mediocre.

states.name: unfocused
states.gap: A's caret origin is x=1899 device px — an odd offset, i.e. 949.5 CSS px at 2x DPR, a half-pixel off the CSS grid, where B's lands clean on 1900/950.0; its centre also sits 5.5px left of the 29px inter-word gap's midpoint (1907) vs B's 4.5px, so it is the more lopsided of the two inside the space.
states.gapTheirs: B's caret stands 1px further from the glyph it trails: 8px of clearance from the 's' ink terminal at x=1892 vs A's 7px, putting it ~3.7px into the ~24.6px space cell where A sits ~2.7px in. The insertion point reads as drifting into the gap rather than docked to the character just typed — at 2x that is a visible half-CSS-pixel of ambiguity about whether you are before or after the space.
states.verdict: These are the same caret with a one-pixel argument between them, and both lose on the thing that actually matters: at #AFE5FB on #F9F9F9 the contrast is roughly 1.29:1, so the caret is a wash of sky against paper — glance away mid-sentence and you will hunt for your place. Both draw it 72px tall against a 72px line pitch, overshooting the ascenders by 19px and the descenders by 16px, so it is a full leading-height slab, not a precise instrument; carets on adjacent lines would touch edge to edge. A takes it only because its bar sits 1px closer to the 's' it follows, which is the difference between a caret attached to your text and one floating in the whitespace. Neither image shows a selection, so the selection colour is simply unshipped in both — and a static frame proves nothing about blink or caret motion, which is exactly where an alive caret is won or lost.
